zones.label: Column 1 running header
zones.note: Lexical cross-check after independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0. Only the supplied page subset was consulted; its headwords are lexical evidence, not a replacement transcription. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Corrections and English review notes are by the external AI reviewer identified in result.json.

lines.note: Hayashi no karasu identifies a crow of the woods. The internal hyphen in Rin-a separates the syllables and agrees with the preceding page's catchword.
Completes the description of the crow as living in scrub or woodland. The gloss gives habitat rather than a precise modern species.
Rinbyō is described as an illness resembling engurria. The unfamiliar historical disease name is retained rather than replaced with a specific modern diagnosis.

runs.text: Hum certo circulo de metal, de que di-

lines.note: Rinbō first denotes a particular metal circle. Di- begins the verb introducing what books say about it.

runs.text: zẽ varias couſas fabuloſas nos liuros. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: Completes dizem and reports that books tell various fabulous things about the object. Itẽ introduces another sense without expanding the abbreviation.

runs.text: Hũa certa marca, ou diuiſa, que ſe pinta nos

lines.note: The second sense is an emblem or device painted on cloth. Pinta has t, not the OCR's pinia.

runs.text: vestidos, ou em outros panos como de armar,

lines.note: Specifies garments and other fabrics, such as hangings, as surfaces carrying the emblem. The physical line continues into &c. below.
Rinbō no maru is given as another expression for the same circular emblem. The circumflex is retained in the repeated form.
Hayashi no ki explains woodland trees or a grove. The Portuguese boſq̃ is an abbreviation and is not expanded in the transcription.
Hayashi no shita means at the foot of or beneath a stand of trees. The noun governed by de baixo follows on the next row.
Completes the location beneath trees or woodland. It belongs to the first Rinca entry.
This separate Rinca means a neighbouring house, as the Japanese tonari no ie makes explicit. The homographic forest entry above is not merged with it.
Kirin no tsuno denotes the horn of the kirin. The Portuguese begins a comparison with another horned animal; a- continues animal below.

runs.text: nimal como vnicorne, ou bada. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: Completes animal and compares it with a unicorn or bada. The source's comparisons are retained without asserting a zoological identity for the kirin.
Introduces the metaphorical sense 'a rare thing' and starts an example about a heart that does not bend. The Japanese co- continues kokoro below.
Says that such a heart is rarer than a kirin's horn. Mare, not the OCR's mate, provides the comparative meaning; Cora- begins the Portuguese translation.

runs.text: ção que ſe não dobra nem vira, he mais raroq̃

lines.note: Completes coração and translates the unwavering heart as rarer than the animal's horn. The abbreviated q̃ remains attached to raro as in the aligned draft; it is not expanded to que.
Finishes the comparison with the horn of the animal discussed in Rincacu. This continuation does not introduce another headword.
Hayashi no aida locates something within the woods. The synonym aruoredo continues the Portuguese description on the following row.
Completes the explanation of Rincan as being within a wood or stand of trees. The short row belongs to the preceding entry.
Hayashi no tori identifies a woodland bird. The circumflex in Rinchô is preserved, distinct from the caron in the following botanical headword.

runs.text: Hũs crauinhos, ou fulas que vem no

lines.note: The headword begins Rin-, not the OCR's Rui-. The Portuguese compares the plants to small carnations and describes when they appear; fulas is retained as printed rather than replaced with a modern botanical name.

runs.text: prĩcipio da primauera. No Cami ſe diz,

lines.note: Says that they appear at the beginning of spring and introduces the Cami regional name. The damaged opening word is read prĩcipio: the abbreviated nasal vowel and traces of the medial letters fit principio, but the middle is poorly inked. The name begins Rin- and continues below.
Completes the regional form Rinchǒqe. The divided name remains on its two physical rows, with the caron in the second segment retained.

Hayashi no uchi means inside the woods. The damaged final glyph of the headword has two stems rather than the draft's i; it is read ǔ, with a very faint mark above. Rinchǔ is also the NINJAL lexical identification. The caron remains less secure than the consonants; no modern spelling is substituted.
Completes the gloss with 'or a cane brake'. The row contains no new Japanese entry.

runs.text: Ida do Rey a algũa parte.

lines.note: Rinkō denotes the king's going to a place. The initial is R, not the OCR's B; the caron is clearly visible.
Rindō is described only as a certain herb. The transcription preserves that nonspecific gloss without adding a modern plant identification.
Teiō no kotoba explains a king's word or utterance. Cotoba has t, not the OCR's r; the shortened nasal ending of Ringuẽ is retained.
Tonari no sato identifies a neighbouring settlement. The synonym is ſato, not ſaro, and the caron distinguishes this headword from the fruit Ringo below.
Supplies 'neighbouring' to complete the preceding description of a settlement. The word is fully within the crop, with the right margin visible.
Ringo is compared to small apples. The scan has initial R rather than B; the historical Portuguese maçaãs is preserved without modernizing its vowel sequence.
Tonari no kuni explains a neighbouring realm. The initial R was dropped by OCR but is fully visible at the left of the native crop.

runs.text: Aruore que dà hũa fruita como

lines.note: Ringo no ki is the tree that bears the fruit compared to small apples above. The Portuguese comparison continues on the next row.
Completes the fruit comparison with the historical diminutive maçãozinhas. The unusual vowel spelling is legible and is not normalized to a modern form.
Ringua is glossed as the time for sleeping. It is a distinct entry between the apple tree and the reluctance-to-give entry.
Oshimi oshimu describes reluctance or begrudging. The Portuguese begins 'having difficulty' and continues difficulda-de below; the printed Japanese form is retained rather than regularized.

runs.text: de de dar, ou emprestar algũa couſa. ¶

lines.note: Completes the definition as reluctance to give or lend something. Go- is the honorific opening of the following Japanese request, not part of the Portuguese sentence.
Completes Go-rinjacu naqu, asking for something to be granted without reluctance. Peço begins the Portuguese translation on this same physical row.

runs.text: vos que me cõcedais iſto ſem repugnãcia, & dò.

lines.note: Finishes the request that the addressee grant the thing without reluctance or regret. The nasal abbreviations and the grave accent in dò are preserved.

runs.text: Recado, ou nouas que contão acrecẽ-

lines.note: Rinjet denotes a report or news embellished by the teller. The nasal abbreviation and line-final division in acrecẽ- are retained.

runs.text: tãdo de ſi varias couſas. Vt,

lines.note: Completes the description of adding details of one's own and gives rinjet o iu as the example. The object marker is printed uo, and yǔ retains its caron.

runs.text: Obra, ou ſeruiço, que ſe impoem, ou

lines.note: Rinji is additional work or service imposed on someone. The Portuguese definition continues across the next row.

runs.text: acrecenta a alguem alem do custumado.

lines.note: Specifies that the work is added beyond what is customary. The source's acrecenta and custumado are retained rather than modernized.
Rinji no quayacu is an example of an extra obligatory duty. The damaged n in Rinjino was mistaken for ù; comparison with the headword and its visible strokes supports n.

runs.text: gatoria, que ſe acrecenta deſta maneira alem do

lines.note: Completes obrigatoria and says that this obligation is added beyond the normal work. The row continues into the next one, with no missing text at its right edge.
Finishes the description of work beyond what a person ordinarily does. Custuma remains in its historical spelling.
Rinjina coto is referred back to the preceding sense. Several poorly inked letters were lost in the OCR's Fnjna, but the initial R and the full sequence Rinjina can be recovered from the native line.
Owari ni nozomu and saigo identify the approach of the end, here the hour of death. The headword's first letter is R, not F; Ho- continues hora on the next row.
Completes the deathbed definition and gives an example meaning that the person's end was good. Te- starts the Portuguese teve below.

runs.text: ue boa morte, ou morreo bẽ. ¶

lines.note: Translates the example as having a good death or dying well, then starts the expression Rinjǔ xǒnen. The Japanese compound remains divided at the printed hyphen.
Completes xǒnen and its explanation as ending or dying well. The Japanese fragment is roman, while the Portuguese gloss is italic.
Teiō no ōse identifies a royal command. The entire Portuguese gloss is italic; the draft's isolated roman e inside Rey was a spurious font split.
Oshimu kokoro introduces jealousy or an envious heart. The Portuguese says that someone is jealous of another person's receiving love or favour, completed below.

runs.text: de outro ſer amado, ou fauorecido. ¶

lines.note: Completes the reason for the jealousy and begins the verbal expression Rin-qi suru. The final hyphen belongs to the Japanese example.
Completes rinki suru, 'to be jealous'. The long s in ſuru is retained as a graphic form, not treated as f.

Rinri, explained by tonari no sato, means a neighbouring place or settlement. The very weak penultimate letter is chosen as r from its low rightward trace and the lexical context, also supported by the NINJAL entry; damage leaves r versus the draft's i a nonblocking uncertainty.
Completes the gloss as a settlement that is nearby. The grave accent in eſtà is retained.
The example repeats rinrin in rinrin to shite, not the OCR's Ronrinto. The first sense describes a fresh or cool condition, whose object follows below.

runs.text: a couſa freſca. ¶ Item, Modo de ſoar al-

lines.note: Completes the freshness sense and introduces a second sense describing the sound of a voice or instrument. The terminal al- belongs to alguma across the line break.
Completes the sounding voice or musical instrument. Inſtrumento has t, not the OCR's i in inſirumento; the long s is preserved.
Tonari explains a neighbouring house or place. The word vizinho divides after vizi without a visible terminal hyphen, so none is supplied.
Completes vizinho and retains the source's S. label. This abbreviated label is not expanded or made a separate entry.
Nagaame explains long-lasting rain. The visible separation in the headword Rin v is retained rather than joined to match the following example's Rinv.
Says that the long rain has not yet cleared. The Portuguese negative is não, not the OCR's mão; Japanese fare represents hare in the supplied romanization.
Completes the statement that the heavy, prolonged rain has not stopped. The historical eſteou and the draft's joined agrande are retained; no lexical modernization is introduced.
Tonari no ie explains a neighbouring house. The headword begins R, not the OCR's B, and its historical vowel sequence is left intact.
Teiō no on-ōse denotes a royal command. Rinxen begins with R rather than B; the honorific von- in the synonym is retained as printed.
Completes 'command of the king'. Rey is Portuguese italic, including its initial capital, not a separate Japanese word.
Rinxi is a royal provision or patent. The ink stain across the Portuguese conjunction does not prevent a usable reading of ou.

runs.text: Sexta lũa, ou mes de Iapão.

lines.note: Rinxô is identified as the sixth Japanese lunar month. The initial R and circumflex are visible; the S. label is retained without expansion.
Wa o meguru and mayou introduce wandering in a circle or going astray. The Portuguese develops the religious sense before contrasting an ordinary conversational use below.

runs.text: errado no caminho da ſaluação, andando em

lines.note: Continues the religious definition as straying from the path of salvation. This is the dictionary's explanatory framing, not an added doctrinal assertion.

Describes a continuous cycle of births and transformations. The dot-like terminal mark after transforma is retained from the aligned draft rather than silently made a hyphen; the word nevertheless continues below.

runs.text: çoens varias. Mas o ſentido ordinario he re-

lines.note: Completes transformaçoens and explicitly contrasts an ordinary meaning. Re- starts repetição on the following row.

runs.text: petição das meſmas couſas que hum ja deuia de

lines.note: Completes repetição, the repetition of things one ought already to have forgotten. The medial t is very poorly inked; petição is the chosen usable reading from its residual stem, the divided re- above and repetir below. This damaged letter remains a nonblocking uncertainty, rather than being silently treated as fully legible.

runs.text: ter eſquecido, ou não deuia de falar. Vt,

lines.note: Adds the alternative of things one ought not to mention at all. Vt introduces the Japanese example on the next line.
The example concerns saying again something in the ordinary repetitive sense just explained. The Portuguese translation starts 'to say again' on the same row.

runs.text: & repetir o que hum deuia de calar para não

lines.note: Continues with repeating what should have been left unsaid. Para não introduces the undesirable effect named on the next row.
Finishes the explanation with avoiding a hurt to someone's feelings. The historical expression and the final &c. are retained without adding a more literal Japanese gloss.
Sono no hayashi describes an orchard or garden. The tilde in Rinyẽ is retained and distinguishes its printed form from Rinyen on the next line.
Fuchi ni nozomu concerns approaching a deep pool or abyss. The Portuguese object follows on the next row.
Completes the description of reaching a deep pool. The old noun pègo and the S. label are kept as printed.
Urokuzu and tsubasa evoke fish and wings, with the Portuguese giving fish and birds. The source's z in Vrocuzu is preserved rather than replaced by a modern spelling.
Completes the pair 'fish and birds' and retains its S. label. It belongs to Rinyocu, not to the following seating entry.
Tonari no za describes an adjacent seat. The location of the neighbouring seats is specified below.

Completes the description of a seat beside another in the zashiki. Zaxiqui is an embedded Japanese room term. The lowercase letters are sloping; the draft's separate upright capital Z is retained because its exact font is less decisive, a nonblocking typography caveat.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de tabernaculo, que fa-

lines.note: Rinzō begins an explanation of a revolving repository or cabinet. The Portuguese fa- continues fazem on the next line.

runs.text: zem andar à roda como eſtante, que ſerue de

lines.note: Completes fazem and describes making the repository rotate like a bookstand. Its function as a library or book repository is specified below.

Says that the revolving repository serves as a library in the temples described by the source as gentile. Liuraria has a dotted i, not nasal ũ. Teras is the embedded temple term. The upright T and less decisive sloping lowercase forms lead to retention of the draft's T/eras font boundary, with a nonblocking typography caveat.
Riǒ and reǒ are alternative forms for a small room or chamber. The lowercase l is the source's vel marker, not a numeral or a bar.
This separate entry means two or both, clarified by futatsu. Riǒ no mimi gives the example of both ears; it is not merged with the homographic room entry.
Translates both ears and adds riǒ no te, both hands. The whole Japanese example is roman; the draft had mistakenly included its initial R within the Portuguese italic span.
Completes Ambas as mãos, the translation of both hands. The abbreviation-free nasal vowel and the physical division Am-bas are retained.
Riǒan first means darkness or gloom. Item introduces a further sense beyond this page; the catchword is separate page furniture, not a continuation merged into this body row.
